chapter_title: Error Handling Alternatives: Error Codes & Assertions

screens.title: Error Handling Alternatives: Error Codes & Assertions
screens.subtitle: When to use error codes, std::error_code, and assert alongside exceptions

narration.text: In this lesson we examine practical, alternative tools to exceptions in C++. You will learn how traditional error codes and the modern std::error_code family complement exceptions, and where assertions fit as a debugging-only safety net. We’ll treat error codes as an explicit, caller-checked contract suitable for expected failures, and std::error_condition as a portable way to map platform-specific errors to abstract conditions. Assertions are different: they verify internal invariants during development and are usually compiled out of release builds. Through concrete examples you will see a file-opening pattern that returns an std::error_code, a divide function that uses assert to enforce preconditions, and a ConfigLoader design that combines all three strategies. Understanding these alternatives matters because choosing the wrong mechanism can either hide failures or add costly overhead. I’ll point out common pitfalls — like forgetting to check a returned error code or misusing assert for user-facing input — and end each section with a practical takeaway so you can decide which tool to use when building robust C++ code. By the end you’ll be able to pick the right error-handling approach for low-level utilities, user-facing operations, and developer-only checks.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Error codes and std::error_code are explicit, caller-managed signals for expected failures; assertions detect programmer bugs during development and disappear in release builds.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Overview
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Error Codes, std::error_code, and Assertions

Learn practical selection rules, read and interpret error codes, and use assertions safely during development.

Duration: 10–12 minutes
In this lesson

Compare mechanisms, inspect std::error_code, and practice a mixed-strategy ConfigLoader.

Coming up

Code walkthroughs for file I/O and assert-driven checks.

Practice

Implement ConfigLoader: return error codes, throw for malformed files, assert invariants.

Why this matters
Choosing the right error mechanism avoids silent failures, unnecessary overhead, and misplaced checks. You'll design clearer contracts between functions and callers.
  • Use error codes when failures are expected and the caller must decide how to continue.
  • Use std::error_code for portable, type-safe system-level reporting and mapping to conditions.
  • Use assert to catch developer mistakes early; do not use it for user input validation.
Key Takeaway

Match the mechanism to the error's nature: expected vs exceptional vs programming bug.

Visual Concept
Cards and mapping lines show where each mechanism fits in a typical application.
Exceptions — Non-local, for truly exceptional failures
Use for catastrophic or unexpected errors where local handling is infeasible.
Error Codes / std::error_code — Explicit, portable reporting
Return a code for expected failures and let the caller make recovery choices.
Assertions — Developer-only invariants
Detect programming errors early; they compile out in release builds.
Explore Key Topics
std::error_code — portable system error reporting
assert — internal sanity checks for developers
Choosing strategies — map expected vs exceptional vs bug

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this lesson

narration.text: These objectives prepare you to choose and apply the right error-handling tool in C++. First, you will compare exceptions with traditional error codes and clearly state when each is appropriate. That means recognizing expected failures versus truly exceptional situations and explaining how each mechanism changes control flow. Second, you will understand std::error_code and std::error_condition: what they represent, how they map platform-specific errors to portable conditions, and how ec. message and ec. value convey diagnostic data. Each objective includes an example so you can see the pattern in code and reason about tradeoffs. The objectives emphasize practical decisions: when to return an error code, when to throw, and when to use assert for internal checks. By the end you will be able to sketch a mixed-handling design for a small utility and justify each choice, which is a valuable skill when building resilient system code or APIs.

narration.text: These practical objectives focus on reading and authoring code. You will interpret a function that returns std::error_code and correctly handle its result in client code, including checking ec and matching against std::errc values. You will write a small assert-based precondition and explain why it compiles out with NDEBUG, so you can rely on it only for development checks. You will also implement a ConfigLoader that demonstrates a deliberate mix: return an error code when a file is missing, throw a custom MalformedConfigFileException for format errors, and assert internal invariants at the start of public methods. Finally, you will explain a typical mistake — forgetting to examine returned error codes — and show mitigation strategies like always assigning the result to a variable and checking it immediately. These skills let you design APIs that are explicit about failure modes and help your team avoid silent runtime errors.

Assign returned std::error_code to a variable and test it with if (ec) rather than ignoring the return value.

screens.title: Exceptions vs Error Codes vs Assertions
screens.subtitle: Different purposes, different guarantees

narration.text: Let’s define the three mechanisms and contrast when each is appropriate. Exceptions are a language facility for non-local error handling. They are best for truly unexpected or catastrophic conditions where normal control flow cannot continue, and they allow error handling to be centralized away from the point of failure. Error codes are explicit return values — integers, enums, or std::error_code — that the caller checks and handles. They suit expected failures that the caller should manage, like file-not-found or permission-denied. Assertions are compile-time-enabled checks used in development to verify internal invariants; when an assert fails it typically aborts the program, signaling a programming bug. A common misconception is treating assertions as lightweight error handling for user input. That is incorrect: asserts are often compiled out in release builds and provide zero production overhead. Another frequent mistake is returning error codes but neglecting to check them; that leads to silent failures. As a concrete example, returning an std::error_code from a file open function lets callers inspect ec. message and decide recovery, while throwing an exception would force unwind handling. A practical rule: use error codes for expected, frequent failure modes, exceptions for exceptional conditions that break normal flow, and asserts strictly for developer-verified invariants. Which combination will you choose for your next utility, and why?

keyIdea.title: Contrast
keyIdea.text: Exceptions for unexpected catastrophic errors; error codes for expected recoverable failures; assertions for developer-only invariants.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Exceptions vs Alternatives
Exceptions

Non-local handler for exceptional errors

Best when the error is rare and cannot be handled locally. Centralizes handling but has unwinding cost.

Misconception: Not ideal for frequent, expected failures.
Error Codes

Explicit, caller-checked returns

Return std::error_code or enums for expected failures. No stack unwinding, but caller must check return values.

Misconception: They are not inherently safer unless consistently checked.
Assertions

Developer-only invariants

Use assert for pre-conditions and invariants during development. They typically disappear in release builds.

Misconception: Do not use asserts for validating user input in production.
Decision hint
Is failure expected and recoverable? → Error code.
Is it a programming bug? → Assert during development.
Is it rare and breaks control flow? → Exception.

screens.title: std::error_code and std::error_condition
screens.subtitle: What each type represents and how they map errors

narration.text: std::error_code is a lightweight, type-safe object representing platform-specific, low-level error conditions. It pairs an integer value with an error category so code can provide rich diagnostics through ec. value and ec. message. std::error_condition is a more abstract concept: it represents portable, generic error meanings that can be mapped from many system-specific error codes. The two work together to let library code present a stable, cross-platform view of failures. For example, many file systems report different codes for missing files, but mapping those codes to std::errc::no_such_file_or_directory via error_condition lets callers write portable checks. A typical pattern is: a function returns std::error_code on failure; the caller checks if (ec) and then can compare ec to a std::errc value or use ec. message for logs. A common pitfall is treating the numeric value as the only source of truth — always inspect the category and use provided comparisons rather than magic numbers. Concrete example: a file open function returns make_error_code(std::errc::no_such_file_or_directory) when the file isn't found. That lets calling code detect this exact condition and provide a clear recovery strategy, such as prompting the user for another path. What mapping would you implement for your platform-specific errors?

keyIdea.title: Error mapping
keyIdea.text: Use std::error_code for system-level errors and std::error_condition to express portable, generic failure meanings.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › std::error_code
std::error_code

Holds a numeric code and category representing platform-specific failures. Check it via if (ec), read ec.message for diagnostics, and use ec.value to log the numeric value.

Concrete example
Return std::make_error_code(std::errc::no_such_file_or_directory) when a requested file is missing so callers can match that condition.
std::error_condition

Represents an abstract, portable error meaning. Use it to map many platform error codes to a single condition, enabling portable comparisons in client code.

Practical note
Prefer comparing to std::errc values or error_condition rather than relying solely on numeric error codes.
Quick checklist
  • Return std::error_code for expected system-level failures.
  • Compare ec against std::errc or use mapping via error_condition for portability.
  • Log ec.message for clear diagnostics.

screens.title: openFileWithErrorHandling — error_code example
screens.subtitle: Walk through returning and interpreting std::error_code

narration.text: Now we walk through a concrete example that returns an std::error_code from a file-open helper. The function attempts to open an ifstream and, if it fails, returns std::make_error_code(std::errc::no_such_file_or_directory). A default-constructed std::error_code signals success. The caller assigns the result to a variable and checks it with if (ec). When ec is true, the caller can log ec. message and compare ec to std::errc values to provide specific recovery behavior, such as telling the user that the file was not found. One common mistake is calling the helper and not storing the error code, which may silently ignore the failure. Another subtlety is to avoid treating numeric values as portable: use std::errc comparisons or map to std::error_condition. In practice, you might prefer returning std::error_code for simple utilities where exceptions would be too costly or where the caller must handle frequent, expected errors. As you read the code panel, notice the minimal control-flow impact and how the pattern makes failure explicit without throwing. Reflect: does your A P I expect callers to check a return value or to handle exceptions? openFileWithErrorHandling — error_code example means return std::error_code for expected file i/o failures; callers check ec and handle specific errc values.. In practical terms, walk through returning and interpreting std::error_code. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pattern
keyIdea.text: Return std::error_code for expected file I/O failures; callers check ec and handle specific errc values.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › openFileWithErrorHandling
Source
<!-- Source code (escaped) --> <#include <iostream>> <#include <string>> <#include <system_error>> // For std::error_code, std::errc <#include <fstream>> // For file operations // Function returning an error code std::error_code openFileWithErrorHandling(const std::string& filename, std::ifstream& file) { file.open(filename); if (!file.is_open()) { // Return a standard error code for file not found return std::make_error_code(std::errc::no_such_file_or_directory); } return std::error_code(); // Default-constructed error_code means no error }
Explanation
  • Default-constructed std::error_code indicates success; any non-zero is an error.
  • std::make_error_code(std::errc::no_such_file_or_directory) provides a portable semantic meaning.
  • Callers should check the returned ec and handle the condition specifically.
  • Avoid treating raw integers as portable diagnostics; use the category and comparisons.
Key Takeaway

This pattern gives explicit, low-overhead failure reporting without exceptions.

screens.title: Interpreting std::error_code in caller code
screens.subtitle: Check, compare, and react to error conditions

narration.text: Understanding how to interpret an std::error_code in caller code completes the pattern. After receiving ec, test it with if (ec) to detect an error. Then use ec. message to present a human-readable message and compare ec with standard errc enumerators such as std::errc::no_such_file_or_directory to handle specific cases. The sample main demonstrates checking ec after trying to open a nonexistent file, logging the message and value, and branching on the specific std::errc value. A misstep here is to only log ec. message and not take corrective action when necessary, or to compare ec. value against platform-specific numbers rather than using std::errc for portability. In the given example, creating a temporary file and reusing the same helper shows how to handle both failure and success paths. Think of ec as a contract: a function says "I may fail for these documented reasons," and the caller must decide whether to retry, prompt the user, or escalate. What recovery paths would you offer for a file-not-found vs permission-denied condition? Interpreting std::error_code in caller code means check ec with if (ec), use ec.message for diagnostics, and compare against std::errc values for portable decisions.. In practical terms, check, compare, and react to error conditions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Caller responsibilities
keyIdea.text: Check ec with if (ec), use ec.message for diagnostics, and compare against std::errc values for portable decisions.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Interpreting ec
Caller pattern (illustrative)
// Example usage pattern (pseudocode)
std::ifstream file;
std::error_code ec = openFileWithErrorHandling("non_existent_file.txt", file);
if (ec) {
  // Log a user-friendly message
  std::cerr << "Error opening file: " << ec.message() << " (Code: " << ec.value() << ")" << std::endl;
  if (ec == std::errc::no_such_file_or_directory) {
    std::cerr << "Specific error: File not found." << std::endl;
    // Offer recovery: prompt for another path
  }
} else {
  // Proceed with file operations
}

// Success case uses the same helper with temp file
Practical tips
  • Always store the returned std::error_code and check it immediately.
  • Prefer comparing ec against std::errc enumerators or error_condition.
  • Use ec.message for logs but not as the only programmatic check.
Common mistake

Ignoring the returned error_code leads to silent failures; enforce check patterns in reviews.

narration.text: Assertions are a development-time tool to verify assumptions your code relies on. In C++ the assert macro from cassert evaluates a boolean expression and, if the expression is false, typically prints a diagnostic and aborts the program. Assertions are appropriate for checking internal invariants and pre/post-conditions that should never be violated in correct code. A classic example is asserting that a denominator is not zero before dividing. The crucial property to remember is that asserts are usually compiled out when NDEBUG is defined, meaning they have no cost in release builds. This makes them unsuitable for checking user input or external data, because those conditions can fail in production and the check would disappear. A typical misconception is to trust that assert prevents all invalid states at runtime; instead, treat assert as a debugging guard that helps you find bugs early, but still validate external inputs with error codes or exceptions in production paths. When you see an assert failure during testing, it signals a programming error that must be fixed, not a recoverable runtime event. Assertions and assert macro means use assert to detect programming errors during development; do not rely on it for production input validation since it is removed in release builds.. In practical terms, enforcing pre-conditions during development. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Assert purpose
keyIdea.text: Use assert to detect programming errors during development; do not rely on it for production input validation since it is removed in release builds.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Assertions
What assert does

Assert evaluates a condition and aborts if false, usually emitting file and line information. It's a developer-focused check, not a user-facing error handler.

Example
int divide(int numerator, int denominator) {
  assert(denominator != 0 && "Denominator cannot be zero!");
  return numerator / denominator;
}
Why it matters
  • Catches programming errors early in testing and development.
  • Has zero runtime cost in release builds when NDEBUG is defined.
  • Do not use assert to check external input or recoverable runtime errors.
Common pitfall

Using assert to validate user data will leave production code unchecked when NDEBUG is active.

screens.title: NDEBUG and assertion behavior across builds
screens.subtitle: How compile-time flags change assert semantics

narration.text: Understanding NDEBUG is essential when relying on assert for development checks. When NDEBUG is defined, the assert macro expands to nothing; the checks and their side effects are removed by the preprocessor. In debug builds asserts help you catch incorrect assumptions and provide immediate feedback. In release builds, those checks vanish, which is why you must not place code with required side effects inside assert expressions. A concrete example in the chapter shows a calculate_sqrt function that asserts the input is non-negative. In debug mode, passing a negative value triggers the assert and alerts the developer. In release mode, the assert is removed and the function will proceed — possibly leading to NaN or other behavior depending on the math library. A practical rule: never use assert for essential validation that must run in production. Instead, validate user inputs with exceptions or error codes. Also, avoid writing expressions with assignment or function calls inside assert that the program depends on, because those calls will disappear when NDEBUG is defined. Finally, use asserts as documentation of internal assumptions so other developers know the intended invariants.

keyIdea.title: NDEBUG impact
keyIdea.text: NDEBUG removes assert checks in release builds; asserts must not perform required side effects or replace production validation.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Assertion Builds
Behavior summary
  • Debug builds: assert checks active, failing an assert aborts with diagnostics.
  • Release builds with NDEBUG: assert checks are compiled out and impose no runtime cost.
  • Do not put critical logic or side-effecting calls inside assert expressions.
Illustrative example
double calculate_sqrt(double value) {
  assert(value >= 0.0 && "Input for square root must be non-negative!");
  return std::sqrt(value);
}
Checklist for developers
  • Use asserts only for developer guarantees and internal invariants.
  • Validate user or external data with error codes or exceptions in production.
  • Document assumptions asserted so reviewers understand the rationale.

screens.title: Designing a mixed-handling ConfigLoader
screens.subtitle: Combine error codes, exceptions, and assert for clarity

narration.text: A real-world design often benefits from mixing strategies. The chapter's ConfigLoader is a good example: it returns an std::error_code when the file does not exist, throws a custom MalformedConfigFileException when content is malformed, and uses assert to guarantee the internal map is initialized. This division is sensible: missing files are expected and callers may handle them differently, so an error_code is appropriate. Malformed files indicate corrupted or invalid input that likely requires different, explicit handling and therefore throw an exception derived from std::runtime_error. The assert ensures internal state is valid during development. When designing such a class, document which conditions produce error codes, which throw, and what invariants are enforced by assert. Also design your public A P I so callers can clearly manage both patterns — for example, check the returned ec first, then wrap load calls in try-catch for exceptions you expect to handle. A common design mistake is mixing these strategies unpredictably across functions; keep a consistent rule set so callers know whether to check returns or catch exceptions. Designing a mixed-handling ConfigLoader means use error codes for expected conditions, exceptions for malformed or unrecoverable data, and asserts for internal invariants in development.. In practical terms, combine error codes, exceptions, and assert for clarity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Mixed strategy
keyIdea.text: Use error codes for expected conditions, exceptions for malformed or unrecoverable data, and asserts for internal invariants in development.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › ConfigLoader Design
Class responsibilities
  • Return std::error_code when the file is missing so callers can recover or retry.
  • Throw MalformedConfigFileException when content is invalid or missing required separators.
  • Assert that internal structures are initialized and never null during development.
Starter code excerpt
// In ConfigLoader::load
assert(configMap_ != nullptr && "Config map should not be null!");
std::ifstream file(filename);
if (!file.is_open()) {
  return std::make_error_code(std::errc::no_such_file_or_directory);
}
// Parse lines; throw MalformedConfigFileException when format is wrong
Design checklist
  • Document which failures are returned and which throw.
  • Ensure callers both check error codes and catch expected exceptions.
  • Keep asserts limited to internal invariants without production side-effects.
Key Takeaway

A consistent mixed approach balances clarity, performance, and robustness.

screens.title: ConfigLoader starter: expected behavior
screens.subtitle: Review the provided starter and expected outcomes for tests

narration.text: The starter ConfigLoader supplies a clear lab scenario. It initializes configMap_ as a unique pointer to avoid null asserts, then implements load to assert the map is valid, open the file, parse each non-empty line by splitting on '=' and fill the map. If the file fails to open, it returns std::errc::no_such_file_or_directory wrapped in an std::error_code. If a line is malformed, or the file is empty, it throws MalformedConfigFileException. The main function in the starter creates three files — valid, empty, and malformed — and tests loading each, handling std::error_code with if (ec) and exceptions with try-catch blocks. The expected outcomes are: non-existent file returns an error code, valid file loads and prints entries, empty file throws MalformedConfigFileException, and malformed file throws the same exception. A common oversight is not cleaning up state between tests, causing false positives; the starter includes cleanup via std::remove for test hygiene. When you implement the missing exception class, ensure it derives from std::runtime_error so callers can catch it by reference and access what(). ConfigLoader starter: expected behavior means non-existent file → error_code; valid file → success; empty or malformed → throw malformedconfigfileexception.. In practical terms, review the provided starter and expected outcomes for tests. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Expected tests
keyIdea.text: Non-existent file → error_code; valid file → success; empty or malformed → throw MalformedConfigFileException.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › ConfigLoader Tests
Starter code excerpt
// TODO: Define MalformedConfigFileException here

class ConfigLoader {
public:
  ConfigLoader() : configMap_(nullptr) {
    configMap_ = std::make_unique<std::map<std::string, std::string>>();
  }

  std::error_code load(const std::string& filename) {
    assert(configMap_ != nullptr && "Config map should not be null!");
    std::ifstream file(filename);
    if (!file.is_open()) {
      return std::make_error_code(std::errc::no_such_file_or_directory);
    }
    // parse lines, throw MalformedConfigFileException for malformed or empty file
  }
};
Test scenarios & outcomes
  • non_existent.txt → expects std::error_code indicating file missing.
  • valid_config.txt → loader returns success and prints key-value pairs.
  • empty_config.txt → loader throws MalformedConfigFileException.
  • malformed_config.txt → loader throws MalformedConfigFileException for invalid lines.
Pro tip

Derive the custom exception from std::runtime_error so callers can catch by reference and inspect what().

screens.title: Implementing and testing ConfigLoader
screens.subtitle: Guided steps and expected diagnostic messages

narration.text: Follow these steps to implement and validate the ConfigLoader behavior. Step one: define MalformedConfigFileException inheriting from std::runtime_error and provide a constructor that forwards the message. Step two: ensure the constructor initializes configMap_ to avoid assert failures. Step three: implement load to open the file, return std::make_error_code(std::errc::no_such_file_or_directory) when opening fails, and parse lines splitting on '='. If a line lacks '=' or is malformed, throw MalformedConfigFileException with a helpful message. Step four: if the file contains no meaningful lines, treat it as malformed and throw. Step five: in main, call load for each test file. Handle error codes with if (ec) and catch MalformedConfigFileException to report the exception what() message. A common debugging tip: print both ec. message() and ec. value() when logging so you get human-readable text and an exact numeric code for correlating with system diagnostics. After tests, remove temporary files to keep a clean workspace. These steps map directly to the starter code and the sample main in the chapter. Implementing and testing ConfigLoader means define exception, ensure config map initialization, return error codes for missing files, throw for malformed content, and test each case.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Pitfalls and best practices
screens.subtitle: Avoiding silent failures and misapplied asserts

narration.text: We close the lessons with concrete pitfalls and a short best-practices checklist. One major pitfall is forgetting to check returned error codes; this produces silent failures that are hard to track down. Enforce a style in your codebase: always assign return codes to a variable and check them immediately, or use helper wrappers that assert a check was performed in debug builds. Another mistake is using assert to validate user input; because asserts disappear in release builds, such checks will not protect production code. Also, avoid placing essential side effects inside assert expressions, as those will vanish with NDEBUG. When mixing exceptions and error codes, document clearly which functions use which strategy so callers know whether to check returns or catch exceptions. For system-level errors prefer std::error_code and compare to std::errc for portability. Finally, when throwing for malformed input, provide clear messages and use exception types derived from std::runtime_error so they integrate with existing catch patterns. Following these practices reduces ambiguity and makes error handling predictable for users of your A P I. Pitfalls and best practices means check error codes consistently, reserve assert for development, document mixed strategies, and prefer std::errc comparisons for portability.. In practical terms, avoiding silent failures and misapplied asserts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Practical rules
keyIdea.text: Check error codes consistently, reserve assert for development, document mixed strategies, and prefer std::errc comparisons for portability.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Pitfalls & Practices
Pitfall: Ignored error codes

Always capture returned std::error_code and check it. Use code reviews to enforce this pattern.

Pitfall: Misusing assert

Don’t use assert for production input validation — it’s for detecting developer bugs in testing.

Best practice: Document behavior

State whether functions return error codes, throw exceptions, or both so callers handle failures correctly.

Short checklist
  • Return error codes for expected, recoverable failures.
  • Throw exceptions for malformed or unrecoverable conditions you want handled via try-catch.
  • Use assert strictly for development invariants and never for production checks.
